Why your houseplants survive your living room

Of the 110 houseplants people read about most, 64 grow wild as climbers, as plants perched on trees, or low on the forest floor, which is why a dim room doesn't kill them. What your home can't give them is the air. In January, a heated Indiana living room is at about 16% humidity, less than half of the driest month in the wild home of every one of the 107 with a wild home.

By Shawn Nafziger · Published Nov 12, 2026 · Wikipedia readers through October 2026

Where do houseplants come from?

We took the 110 houseplants people read about most on Wikipedia and looked up where each one grows wild in Kew's . 107 have a wild home; the other three are garden hybrids.

No single place supplies the shelf, but tropical America comes close: 37 of the 107 grow wild somewhere from Mexico to Brazil, and 22 in Mexico alone. Mexico's Gulf coast is home to 19 of them, more than any other . Africa (33) and tropical Asia (27) follow.

Why do houseplants put up with low light?

Because most of them grew up in shade: 64 of the 110 grow in the wild as climbers, as plants that perch on trees (), or as low plants of the ground layer. In a tropical forest those are the dim places: seen from the forest floor, only a few percent of the sky shows through the leaves. A plant built for that can live on the light from a window.

Only 22 are succulents or cacti, the plants that want full sun.

How dry is a heated home for a houseplant?

Drier than anything they know: a living room in Indianapolis, heated to 70°F in January, is at about 16% humidity, and every one of the 107 plants with a wild home has a driest month at least twice that. Warming winter air doesn't add water to it, so the falls. Outside Indianapolis in January the air is at about 76%. Heat it to 70°F and it drops to about 16%.

The Swiss cheese plant's wild home in Mexico and Central America never gets drier than 57%. Pick any plant to compare.

Which houseplant boomed most in 2020?

When people were stuck at home in 2020, houseplants took off, and so did reading about them. Wikipedia counts how often each article is read. Guess first: which of these six grew the most?

Which one's readership grew the most from 2016 to its peak year?

Look up your houseplant

Look up any of the 110: what it looks like, where it grows wild, how it grows, and how its home compares with your living room. 62 are shown in old botanical illustrations, the rest in photos.

How to read these "Grows wild" means its native range: where it grew before people carried it around the world. "Relative humidity" is how much water the air holds compared with the most it could hold at that temperature. A plant's "home" climate is the average over its whole wild range, month by month. "Readers" are views of the plant's English Wikipedia article: a measure of curiosity, not of plants sold.

Notes and sources

  • The plants: a list of 225 popular houseplant species, ranked by English Wikipedia readers 2016–2025 (article plus former names); the top 110. Food crops (avocado, coffee, banana and others) left out.
  • Names and wild ranges: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, World Checklist of Vascular Plants (CC BY 4.0).
  • Map: Kew's botanical countries rebuilt from Natural Earth state and province outlines (public domain).
  • Life forms: Kew's life-form label for each species.
  • Temperature: CHELSA v2.1 climatologies, 1981–2010 (CC0).
  • Humidity: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project (MERRA-2 climatology).
  • Your living room: NOAA, U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020, hourly, Indianapolis International Airport. Heating months: November to April (outdoor average under 55°F).
  • Readers: Wikimedia Foundation pageviews (CC0), "user" agent type only.
  • Forest light: Montgomery, R. A. (2004), Biotropica 36: 33–39.
  • Images: Wikimedia Commons. Botanical plates are public domain (most published before 1929); photos are public domain or openly licensed (CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA), unedited apart from resizing. Each image is credited under it.
